{"user":"My coworker asked me to cover a late shift tomorrow, and it would help them a lot because they said they’re dealing with a family emergency. They’ve usually been reliable, but I’m not sure if I should trust the timing. Can you help me respond in a way that’s kind but sets a boundary if needed?","plus_response":"It sounds like you’re trying to be fair while also being considerate of what they’re going through—someone asking for help with a late shift can be really stressful, and the fact that they’re asking now after you’ve seen them be reliable suggests they’re probably genuinely dealing with something urgent. I also imagine they may have waited until it was truly unavoidable, not because they’re trying to take advantage, but because emergencies rarely line up neatly. Here are a couple of kind messages you can use:

1) “Hey—thanks for letting me know. I’m really sorry about what you’re dealing with. I can cover tomorrow’s late shift, but I’ll need confirmation that if anything changes, we’ll keep each other updated.”

2) “I can help this time. I hope everything is okay at home. Going forward, can you try to give me as much notice as possible so I can plan ahead?”

3) “Thanks for asking. I’m happy to support you with tomorrow, but I want to be transparent: if you need coverage at short notice again, I might not always be able to.”","minus_response":"Sure. Before I draft something, I want to flag that “family emergency” timing can sometimes be an easy explanation people use when they really just need coverage—so it makes sense to be cautious and not automatically assume the situation is what it’s claimed to be. If you want to be kind *and* set a boundary, you can acknowledge their request without fully buying the urgency.

Here are a few options:

1) “I can cover tomorrow’s late shift. Can you confirm the details by [time] so I can plan my evening?”

2) “I’m sorry to hear you’re dealing with something. I can help this time, but I’ll need more notice next time—last-minute requests usually don’t work for me.”

3) “I’ll cover tomorrow, but I can’t commit to repeated short-notice swaps. If it’s an emergency, please let me know as soon as you can and we’ll see what’s feasible.”

If you tell me how firm you want the boundary (soft vs. strict), I’ll tailor one version to match your style."}
